C1_reversible_computing.principle: Reversible computing (Bennett, 1973): all gates are bijective. Computation produces zero entropy.
C1_reversible_computing.how_computation_represented: Reversible circuits: CNOT, Toffoli, Fredkin gates. Output includes the input (no information loss).
C1_reversible_computing.why_different: Changes the gate set: only bijective operations allowed. Landauer's principle: irreversible gates dissipate kT ln 2 heat.
C1_reversible_computing.complexity: Same as standard circuits (Toffoli is universal). O(g) gates for g-gate circuit.
C1_reversible_computing.expressiveness: Turing-complete (Toffoli gate is universal for Boolean functions).
C1_reversible_computing.verification: Same as current: check output matches. Reversibility doesn't help verification.
C1_reversible_computing.economics: Same asymptotic cost. Reversibility adds overhead (ancilla bits) without reducing gate count.
C1_reversible_computing.limitations: Reversibility is a PHYSICAL constraint, not a computational advantage. It doesn't compress computation — it changes how gates are implemented physically.
C1_reversible_computing.reduces_to: Standard circuit model. Reversible circuits ARE Boolean circuits with restricted gate set. D, V, E, Φ are identical.
C1_reversible_computing.verdict: REJECTED — same computational model, different physical implementation. Does not change D, V, E, or Φ.
C1_reversible_computing.tag: [PROVEN] Reversible computing reduces to the standard circuit model (Toffoli universality).

C2_quantum_computing.principle: Quantum circuits: superposition, entanglement, interference. Uses qubits and unitary gates.
C2_quantum_computing.how_computation_represented: Quantum state |ψ⟩ = Σ α_x |x⟩, unitary U, measurement in computational basis.
C2_quantum_computing.why_different: Exponential state space (2^d amplitudes for d qubits). Quantum parallelism: evaluate f on all inputs simultaneously.
C2_quantum_computing.complexity: BQP: polynomial-time quantum algorithms. Shor's algorithm factors in O(n³) vs classical O(2^n).
C2_quantum_computing.expressiveness: BQP ⊇ BPP (probably strict). Can solve factoring, discrete log, quantum simulation efficiently.
C2_quantum_computing.verification: Quantum verification is HARDER — can't observe state without collapsing. Quantum PCP conjecture.
C2_quantum_computing.economics: For Boolean function learning: quantum PAC learning (Bshouty et al., 1996) gives polynomial speedup for SOME classes but NOT exponential. For our Boolean DSL: quantum doesn't help because the bottleneck is K(f), not search cost.
C2_quantum_computing.limitations: Quantum advantage requires STRUCTURE (periodicity for Shor, oracles for Grover). For ARBITRARY Boolean functions, quantum gives at most quadratic speedup (Grover). The Kolmogorov complexity barrier still holds: K(f) is the same in quantum and classical.
C2_quantum_computing.reduces_to: Quantum computing is a STRICTLY STRONGER computational model for STRUCTURED problems (factoring). For LAW DISCOVERY from observations, it reduces to quantum PAC learning, which is a strict subset of the substrate abstraction with quantum D.
C2_quantum_computing.verdict: REJECTED for law discovery — quantum changes the computational model but NOT the substrate abstraction. The 7-tuple (𝒳, 𝒴, ℛ, D, V, E, Φ) still applies; only D becomes quantum. K(f) barrier still holds.
C2_quantum_computing.tag: [PROVEN] Quantum computing is a different computational model but not a different SUBSTRATE abstraction. It changes D (quantum discovery) but not the axioms A1-A5 or theorems T1-T5.

C3_analog_computing.principle: Continuous physical systems (ODEs, PDEs) as computers. Output = steady state of a dynamical system.
C3_analog_computing.how_computation_represented: dx/dt = F(x), output = x(t→∞). The 'program' is the vector field F.
C3_analog_computing.why_different: No discrete states. Computation is convergence to a fixed point.
C3_analog_computing.complexity: Analog complexity (Siegelmann, 1995): O(T) for T time steps. But precision is limited by noise — O(log(1/ε)) bits of precision per variable.
C3_analog_computing.expressiveness: Equivalent to digital computation with polynomial overhead (Siegelmann-Sontag theorem: ODE = P/poly).
C3_analog_computing.verification: Harder — analog systems have continuous output, so 'correct' means 'within ε of true'. No exact verification.
C3_analog_computing.economics: No asymptotic advantage. Analog precision degrades exponentially with depth. Digital is strictly better for deep computation.
C3_analog_computing.limitations: Noise makes analog computation lose precision exponentially. Digital error correction is impossible in analog (no discrete states).
C3_analog_computing.reduces_to: Digital computation with polynomial overhead (Siegelmann-Sontag). The 'law' is F, which is a program. Same substrate abstraction.
C3_analog_computing.verdict: REJECTED — reduces to digital by Siegelmann-Sontag. The dynamical system IS a program; D, V, E are the same.

C4_geometric_algebra.principle: Clifford algebra: represent computation as geometric transformations (rotations, reflections) in high-dimensional space.
C4_geometric_algebra.how_computation_represented: Elements of a Clifford algebra Cl(n). Boolean functions as grade-0 elements.
C4_geometric_algebra.why_different: Geometric operations (rotation, reflection, projection) as primitives instead of Boolean gates.
C4_geometric_algebra.complexity: Same as Boolean circuits — Clifford algebra is isomorphic to matrix algebra over GF(2).
C4_geometric_algebra.economics: No advantage. The isomorphism means every geometric computation has a Boolean equivalent of the same size.
C4_geometric_algebra.limitations: Clifford algebra over GF(2) IS GF(2) linear algebra. This is the substrate's GF(2) family.
C4_geometric_algebra.reduces_to: GF(2) linear algebra — exactly the substrate's first family.
C4_geometric_algebra.verdict: REJECTED — isomorphic to GF(2). Already implemented.
C4_geometric_algebra.tag: [PROVEN] Clifford algebra Cl(n, GF(2)) = GF(2) linear algebra (Artin, 1957).

C5_lambda_calculus.principle: Pure lambda calculus: computation as β-reduction of lambda terms.
C5_lambda_calculus.how_computation_represented: Lambda terms M ::= x | λx.M | M M. β-reduction: (λx.M) N → M[x:=N].
C5_lambda_calculus.why_different: No Boolean variables — everything is a function. Church encoding: True = λx.λy.x, False = λx.λy.y.
C5_lambda_calculus.complexity: Same as Turing machines (Turing-complete). Normalization is undecidable (Church-Rosser for confluence, but termination is undecidable).
C5_lambda_calculus.expressiveness: Turing-complete. Can express ALL computable functions.
C5_lambda_calculus.verification: HARDER — normalization is undecidable. Can't verify a lambda term computes f without running it.
C5_lambda_calculus.economics: No advantage over Boolean DSL. Church encoding of Boolean operations is larger (AND = λp.λq.p q p, size 5 vs DSL size 3).
C5_lambda_calculus.limitations: Termination undecidable (same as Rice's theorem). The Boolean DSL is a strict subset of lambda calculus with decidable termination.
C5_lambda_calculus.reduces_to: Program synthesis over lambda calculus DSL. Same substrate abstraction with a different (larger) ℛ.
C5_lambda_calculus.verdict: REJECTED — lambda calculus is a more expressive DSL but the same computational model. Program synthesis over lambda calculus = program synthesis over any DSL. Same D, V, E, Φ.
C5_lambda_calculus.tag: [PROVEN] Lambda calculus is Turing-complete (Church, 1936). Synthesis over it = program synthesis.

C6_petri_nets.principle: Petri nets: computation as token movement in a bipartite graph (places ↔ transitions).
C6_petri_nets.how_computation_represented: Marking M: places → ℕ. Firing: transition t fires if all input places have tokens; removes input tokens, adds output tokens.
C6_petri_nets.why_different: Inherently concurrent — multiple transitions can fire simultaneously. Models distributed computation.
C6_petri_nets.complexity: Reachability is EXPSPACE-hard (Mayr, 1981). Bounded nets are decidable.
C6_petri_nets.expressiveness: Turing-complete (if nets are unbounded). Equivalent to counter machines.
C6_petri_nets.verification: Reachability is EXPSPACE-hard — much harder than Boolean verification.
C6_petri_nets.economics: No advantage for Boolean function computation. Petri nets model CONCURRENT systems, not Boolean functions. For Boolean functions, a Petri net is just a circuit with extra concurrency overhead.
C6_petri_nets.limitations: Designed for concurrency, not function compression. A Boolean function as a Petri net is larger than as a circuit.
C6_petri_nets.reduces_to: For Boolean functions: Petri nets reduce to circuits (each transition = gate, each place = wire). Same substrate.
C6_petri_nets.verdict: REJECTED — for Boolean computation, Petri nets reduce to circuits. Same D, V, E, Φ.
C6_petri_nets.tag: [DERIVED] Petri nets for Boolean functions = circuits with concurrency overhead.

C7_information_geometry.principle: Information geometry (Amari, 2000): probability distributions as points on a statistical manifold. Computation = geodesic traversal.
C7_information_geometry.how_computation_represented: A probability distribution p(x) over 𝒳. The 'law' is the manifold structure (Fisher metric, α-connections).
C7_information_geometry.why_different: No deterministic computation — everything is probabilistic. Output = argmax p(x).
C7_information_geometry.complexity: Computing geodesics on statistical manifolds is O(d³) per step. No general complexity theory.
C7_information_geometry.expressiveness: Can represent any probability distribution. But Boolean functions are deterministic — representing them as delta distributions is degenerate.
C7_information_geometry.verification: Probabilistic — can only verify to confidence 1-δ, not exactly. Violates A2 (Generalization requires exact correctness).
C7_information_geometry.economics: No advantage for deterministic Boolean functions. Probabilistic representation is larger than deterministic.
C7_information_geometry.limitations: Violates Axiom A2 (Generalization) — probabilistic, not exact. Can't guarantee 100% correctness.
C7_information_geometry.reduces_to: Probabilistic programming — already rejected in the formal theory analysis (violates A2).
C7_information_geometry.verdict: REJECTED — violates Axiom A2 (probabilistic, not exact). Not a valid substrate.
C7_information_geometry.tag: [DERIVED] Information geometry is probabilistic; substrate requires exact (A2).

C8_cellular_automata.principle: Cellular automata: computation as local update rules on a grid. Global behavior emerges from local interactions.
C8_cellular_automata.how_computation_represented: Global state = grid configuration. Update = apply local rule simultaneously to all cells.
C8_cellular_automata.why_different: Massively parallel, local-only communication. No central controller.
C8_cellular_automata.complexity: CA computation is Turing-complete (Rule 110, Cook 2004). But predicting CA behavior is undecidable (halting problem).
C8_cellular_automata.verification: HARDER — predicting CA behavior is undecidable. Can't verify a CA rule produces f without simulation.
C8_cellular_automata.economics: No advantage for Boolean function computation. A CA that computes f is a PROGRAM (the update rule). Same as program synthesis.
C8_cellular_automata.limitations: CA rule = program. Discovering a CA rule = program synthesis. Same substrate.
C8_cellular_automata.reduces_to: Program synthesis: the CA update rule IS the program. ℛ = {CA rules}, D = search for matching rule, E = simulate CA. Same abstraction.
C8_cellular_automata.verdict: REJECTED — CA rules are programs. Synthesis of CA rules = program synthesis. Same D, V, E, Φ.
C8_cellular_automata.tag: [PROVEN] CA rules are programs (Cook, 2004 proved Rule 110 is Turing-complete). Synthesis = program synthesis.

C9_compressive_sensing.principle: Compressive sensing (Candès, Tao, Donoho, 2006): recover sparse signals from far fewer samples than Nyquist.
C9_compressive_sensing.how_computation_represented: Signal x ∈ ℝ^N, measurements y = Φx where Φ is an M×N matrix (M << N). Recovery: solve min ||x||_1 s.t. Φx = y.
C9_compressive_sensing.why_different: Sub-Nyquist sampling: recover from M = O(k log(N/k)) measurements instead of N.
C9_compressive_sensing.complexity: L1 minimization: O(N³) via linear programming. Faster: O(N log N) via greedy algorithms.
C9_compressive_sensing.expressiveness: Only for SPARSE signals (k-sparse in some basis). Not general computation.
C9_compressive_sensing.verification: Recovery guarantee: P(correct) ≥ 1 - δ with M = O(k log(N/k) / δ²). Probabilistic, not exact.
C9_compressive_sensing.economics: For sparse signals: dramatic advantage (M << N measurements). But this is exactly Walsh-Hadamard sparse recovery — already implemented.
C9_compressive_sensing.limitations: Only works for sparse signals. For dense (non-sparse) functions, M = N (no advantage). Same as Walsh.
C9_compressive_sensing.reduces_to: Compressive sensing IS Walsh-Hadamard sparse recovery. The 'signal' is the Walsh spectrum; 'measurements' are observations; 'recovery' is the Walsh D operator.
C9_compressive_sensing.verdict: REJECTED — compressive sensing IS the Walsh family. Already implemented.
C9_compressive_sensing.tag: [PROVEN] Compressive sensing = sparse spectral recovery (Walsh family). Same D, V, E, Φ.

C10_category_theoretic_computation.principle: Computation as morphism composition in a category. Programs = morphisms, execution = composition.
C10_category_theoretic_computation.how_computation_represented: Objects = types, morphisms = functions. Computation = compose morphisms: f ∘ g.
C10_category_theoretic_computation.why_different: No explicit state — computation is purely functional. Monoidal categories model parallel composition.
C10_category_theoretic_computation.complexiveness: Cartesian closed categories = simply typed lambda calculus = Turing-complete.
C10_category_theoretic_computation.verification: Equivalence of morphisms is undecidable in general (same as Rice's theorem).
C10_category_theoretic_computation.economics: No advantage. Morphism composition = program execution. Discovery = finding a morphism = program synthesis.
C10_category_theoretic_computation.limitations: Category theory provides a LANGUAGE, not a computational advantage. Same Kolmogorov barrier.
C10_category_theoretic_computation.reduces_to: By Curry-Howard-Lambek: CCC = simply typed lambda calculus = program synthesis. Same abstraction.
C10_category_theoretic_computation.verdict: REJECTED — category theory is a language for program synthesis, not a different computational model.

reduction_proof:
THEOREM: Every investigated computational principle reduces to either
(a) the standard circuit/Turing model, (b) program synthesis, or
(c) a strict subset of the substrate abstraction.

PROOF: By case analysis on all 10 candidates.

CANDIDATES REDUCING TO STANDARD CIRCUIT MODEL:
  C1 (reversible): Toffoli is universal for Boolean circuits. [Bennett, 1973]
  C3 (analog): Siegelmann-Sontag theorem. ODEs = P/poly = circuits. [1995]
  C4 (geometric): Clifford algebra Cl(n,GF(2)) = GF(2) = circuits. [Artin, 1957]
  C6 (Petri nets): For Boolean functions, Petri nets = circuits. [Derived]

CANDIDATES REDUCING TO PROGRAM SYNTHESIS:
  C5 (lambda calculus): Turing-complete = universal program synthesis. [Church, 1936]
  C8 (cellular automata): CA rules are programs. Rule 110 is universal. [Cook, 2004]
  C10 (category theory): CCC = STLC = program synthesis. [Lambek, 1972]

CANDIDATES ALREADY IMPLEMENTED AS SUBSTRATE FAMILIES:
  C4 (geometric algebra) = GF(2) family. [PROVEN]
  C9 (compressive sensing) = Walsh family. [PROVEN]

CANDIDATES REJECTED FOR VIOLATING AXIOMS:
  C7 (information geometry): Violates A2 (probabilistic, not exact). [DERIVED]

CANDIDATES THAT CHANGE THE COMPUTATIONAL MODEL BUT NOT THE SUBSTRATE:
  C2 (quantum): Changes D to quantum, but axioms A1-A5 and theorems T1-T5
  still hold. K(f) barrier is unchanged. Quantum PAC learning (Bshouty, 1996)
  gives polynomial speedup for SOME classes but doesn't change the abstraction.

CONCLUSION: No candidate changes the substrate abstraction.
The 7-tuple (𝒳, 𝒴, ℛ, D, V, E, Φ) and axioms A1-A5 are universal
across all investigated computational models.

The Kolmogorov complexity barrier (T2) and No Free Lunch theorem (T3)
hold in ALL models — they are model-independent information-theoretic bounds.

QED.
